title: Two streams and an exit code

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Add `2> /dev/null` (or `2> $null` in PowerShell) to see only standard output, and print the exit code with `echo $?` (or `$LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell).

tasks.title: Put results on standard output and messages on standard error
tasks.description:
Send each kind of text to its own stream.

- `out.result` prints on standard output; `out.note`, a message for the person at the terminal, prints on standard error
- an error ends in one line on standard error, `orders: ` and its message, with nothing on standard output and no stack trace
- help and the version are what was asked for, so they stay on standard output

The check runs `node orders.js` on order files of its own and reads standard output and standard error apart: `check` with problems, `count`, an unknown flag, a file that is not there, and `--help`.
nextSteps: Run `node orders.js check orders/press-2.txt 2> /dev/null` (PowerShell: `2> $null`): only what is on standard output stays.
Change `out.note` and the line in the `catch` at the bottom of `orders.js`.
Run the command again: only the two problem lines should stay.
hints: `console.log` writes to standard output and `console.error` to standard error. Both look the same in a terminal, which is why the mix-up hides until someone pipes the output.
Ask of each line: is it what the person asked for, or something said to them about it? The summary of `check` and every error are said to the person.

tasks.title: End with an exit code other programs can act on
tasks.description:
Make the tool end with an exit code that says how it went.

- `0` when all went well, help and the version included
- `1` when `check` found a problem: the run function returns `false` then
- `2` when the tool could not do what it was asked: a flag, a value or a command it does not know, or a file it cannot read
- everything the tool printed reaches the reader before it ends

The check stands in for a pipe that takes a moment: what the tool writes is handed over a little later, as on a pipe on Linux or macOS. A tool that stops with `process.exit()` right after printing loses what it had not handed over yet.

The check runs `node orders.js` with checks that pass and fail, a long list, and each kind of mistake, and reads the exit code and everything that arrived.
nextSteps: Read "Exit codes" and "Ending without losing output" in the lesson.
Make `main` give back the code for how it went, and the `catch` the code for an error.
Set the code so the tool still ends by itself, once everything is written.
hints: The run function of a command already returns whether all was well. Help and the version are a success too.
`process.exit(code)` stops the tool at once, even when part of what it printed is still on its way. `process.exitCode` only says which code to end with, when the tool ends by itself.
Return `ok ? 0 : 1` from `main` after running the command, and `0` after help or the version. Then `process.exitCode = await main(process.argv.slice(2))`, and `process.exitCode = 2` in the `catch`.

tasks.title: Print JSON for a program with --json
tasks.description:
Add `--json`, so another program can read the results without cutting text apart.

- `json` is a switch in `FLAGS` in `src/flags.js`, with an `about` that says what it does
- every command takes it: add it to the `flags` of each entry in `COMMANDS`, and the help shows it
- with `--json`, each result is printed on standard output as one line: the JSON of the value `out.result` was given for it, and nothing else
- notes and errors stay plain text on standard error

For example, `node orders.js count --by paper --json orders/press-1.txt` prints one line for each paper:

```
{"paper":"cotton","orders":2}
```

The check runs each command with `--json` on order files of its own, reads each line of standard output as JSON and compares it with the values the shop's functions give.
nextSteps: Add the flag to `FLAGS` and to each command, and run `node orders.js list --help`.
Read "Output for programs" in the lesson.
Make `out.result` print the value as JSON when the flag is on.
hints: `out` needs to know the flags, so it has to be made where the flags are known: inside `main`, after `readArgs`.
`JSON.stringify(value)` gives one line with no spaces. Giving it more arguments spreads the JSON over several lines, which a program reading a line at a time cannot use.

`json: { about: 'one JSON value on each line, for programs' }` in `FLAGS`, `'json'` in each command's `flags`, and in `main`: `result: (text, value) => console.log(flags.json ? JSON.stringify(value) : text)`.
